clinicalPearls: Caused by biallelic variants in AMPD1 encoding the muscle-specific isoform of AMP deaminase, the enzyme that deaminates adenosine monophosphate to inosine monophosphate within the purine nucleotide cycle during exercise.
The commonest inherited defect of the purine nucleotide cycle in skeletal muscle; a single recurrent nonsense variant accounts for the great majority of pathogenic alleles in many populations.

Presents as exercise-induced myalgia, early fatigue and cramping, sometimes with exertional rhabdomyolysis and myoglobinuria; many homozygotes remain wholly asymptomatic, so the biochemical defect and clinical disease are often dissociated.

Distinguish the primary (inherited) form from acquired secondary deficiency, in which reduced enzyme activity is a bystander finding alongside another established neuromuscular disorder such as an inflammatory or dystrophic myopathy.

The ischaemic (or non-ischaemic) forearm exercise test characteristically shows a normal lactate rise but a blunted or absent rise in ammonia, the mirror image of the flat lactate seen in glycogenoses.
Resting serum creatine kinase may be normal or only mildly elevated between attacks, so a normal value does not exclude the diagnosis.

Confirm with muscle biopsy histochemical staining for AMP deaminase activity or biochemical assay, and with AMPD1 gene testing; management is supportive with graded activity, avoidance of exhaustive exertion and attention to hydration around exercise.
Anecdotal reports describe symptomatic benefit from oral ribose supplementation, but evidence is limited and it is not established therapy.
reference.pathophysiology: Myoadenylate deaminase deficiency results from loss-of-function variants in AMPD1 on chromosome 1p13, which encodes the muscle-specific (isoform M) subunit of adenosine monophosphate deaminase. Within contracting skeletal muscle this enzyme drives the purine nucleotide cycle by deaminating AMP to inosine monophosphate with release of ammonia, a reaction that helps maintain a favourable adenylate energy charge by removing AMP and displacing the adenylate kinase equilibrium towards adenosine triphosphate regeneration, while also feeding the tricarboxylic acid cycle through anaplerotic replenishment of fumarate. When muscle AMP deaminase activity is absent, vigorous or sustained exercise leads to inefficient regeneration of high-energy phosphates and excessive loss of adenine nucleotides, manifesting as premature fatigue, cramping and, in some individuals, myofibre breakdown. A single recurrent premature stop variant is the predominant disease allele; the marked variability in whether homozygotes develop symptoms is thought to reflect residual or compensatory ammonia-generating pathways and modifier effects, explaining why the enzyme defect is frequently detected incidentally.
additionalDifferentials: McArdle disease (myophosphorylase deficiency) and other glycogen-storage myopathies, in which the forearm test shows a flat lactate but a normal ammonia rise
Carnitine palmitoyltransferase II deficiency and other fatty-acid oxidation defects causing exertional rhabdomyolysis
Secondary (acquired) AMP deaminase deficiency accompanying an inflammatory or dystrophic myopathy
Recurrent exertional rhabdomyolysis due to RYR1-related or malignant-hyperthermia-susceptible myopathy
Benign exertional cramp syndromes and simple deconditioning
additionalInvestigations: Ischaemic or non-ischaemic forearm exercise test measuring paired venous lactate and ammonia responses
Muscle biopsy with histochemical staining for AMP deaminase activity, plus routine histology to exclude another myopathy
Biochemical assay of AMP deaminase activity in muscle tissue
Targeted AMPD1 sequencing, including testing for the common recurrent variant
Serum creatine kinase at rest and after exertion, with urine myoglobin during acute episodes
Broader metabolic myopathy panel (acylcarnitines, other enzyme assays) when the phenotype is atypical
redFlags: Pigmented (tea-coloured) urine after exertion indicating myoglobinuria and possible rhabdomyolysis
Marked post-exercise weakness with grossly elevated creatine kinase suggesting significant muscle breakdown
Features of acute kidney injury complicating a rhabdomyolysis episode
Rapidly progressive fixed weakness, which points away from this disorder towards an alternative myopathy
reference.prognosis: Overall prognosis is good and life expectancy is normal, with many enzyme-deficient individuals remaining asymptomatic throughout life. Symptomatic patients typically experience exercise-limited myalgia and occasional rhabdomyolysis that are managed conservatively, though severe exertional episodes rarely carry the usual complications of myoglobinuric acute kidney injury.
pitfalls: Interpreting an incidentally low muscle enzyme activity as the cause of symptoms without excluding a coexisting primary myopathy (the secondary/acquired form).
Excluding the diagnosis on the basis of a normal resting creatine kinase, which is common between episodes.
Misattributing a flat ammonia response to a technically inadequate forearm test; venous sampling and effort must be validated by the paired lactate rise.
Assuming that homozygosity for the common variant guarantees clinical disease, given the frequent asymptomatic state.
Overlooking hydration and rhabdomyolysis risk when advising patients about strenuous or competitive exercise.
